claims.text: The low hardness of single-phase equimolar CoCrFeNiTi is governed by enhanced dislocation mobility.
The low strength of single-phase equimolar CoCrFeNiTi is governed by enhanced dislocation mobility.
The single-phase solid solution lacks strong lattice distortions that would impede dislocations.
The single-phase solid solution lacks precipitate barriers that would impede dislocations.
The absence of strong lattice distortions and secondary-phase barriers permits relatively easy dislocation glide.
Relatively unobstructed dislocation motion reduces work hardening.
Relatively unobstructed dislocation motion leads to lower hardness and strength.
Lowering the test temperature should impede dislocation motion.
Increasing the strain rate should impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion at cryogenic temperature should increase yield strength and hardness relative to room-temperature testing.
Impeded dislocation motion at higher strain rates should increase yield strength and hardness relative to low-strain-rate testing.
At room temperature and low strain rates, the alloy should exhibit high dislocation mobility accompanied by low hardness and yield strength.
Room-temperature, low-strain-rate tests consistently show favorable plasticity and machinability in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
Room-temperature, low-strain-rate tests consistently show relatively low hardness and strength in equimolar CoCrFeNiTi.
The proposed mechanism is restricted to equimolar or nearly equimolar CoCrFeNiTi in a single-phase solid-solution state without secondary precipitates or phase separation.
Subtle local chemical ordering may influence dislocation motion.

contradictions.description: The conditions state that thermal-activation effects will be isolated from dislocation mobility, but the mechanism uses temperature as an intervention intended to change dislocation mobility. Thermal activation and dislocation mobility are therefore treated as separable in one field and causally linked in another.
